title: Executive Function Task Laboratory
summary: Predict which processes each of four executive tasks requires, then reveal the weights behind them. Change six capacities and see what a single summary score hides.
learningObjectives: Explain why every executive task requires several processes at once.
Show that the mapping from a lowest task score to a reduced capacity is many-to-one.
Explain why processing speed and sustained effort must be accounted for before any executive interpretation.
Describe what a single summary score hides about a speed-accuracy trade-off.
State why 'executive function' is a description of a set of demands rather than a mechanism.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it. Nobody performs the tasks and no score means anything about the reader.
accessibilityNotes: Native radio, checkbox, range and button controls; the capacity sliders announce meaningful values such as 'Inhibition at 35 per cent of the typical level' and the strategy slider announces 'leaning towards speed'. Each experiment has its own pinned primary chart and the inactive one is hidden, so only one primary is ever visible. Both charts are hidden from assistive technology and each carries a visible sentence inside its own figure stating the same information in words - every weight and every capacity ticked in experiment 1, every score and the lowest task in experiment 2 - because the pinned chart stays on screen while the tables scroll away. Each chart is also paired with a visible table: in experiment 1 a prediction-against-model table for every capacity, in experiment 2 a table giving each task's summary score with accuracy and speed shown separately for the timed tasks. The learner's prediction is drawn as a tick shape rather than a colour and repeated as yes or no in the table; every bar prints its own number; the lowest task is named in the interpretation as well as filled differently. A stage track marks progress. All changes announce through the shell's polite live region. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Why no executive task is pure, why a low score identifies nothing on its own, and what a summary score hides about strategy
simulationNotes: Four invented tasks and six invented capacities. Each task is a set of weights on the capacities; each capacity has a level between 0 and 1 where 1 is typical; the simulated score is 100 times the weighted sum of levels over the sum of weights, so all capacities at 1 give 100 on every task. The weight matrix - inhibition, switching, updating, planning, speed, effort - is 0.90, 0.10, 0.15, 0, 0.70, 0.50 for the colour-word task; 0.50, 0.90, 0.40, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50 for the rule-change task; 0.30, 0.10, 0.90, 0, 0.50, 0.60 for the running-total task; and 0.50, 0.20, 0.60, 0.90, 0.15, 0.40 for the disc puzzle. No row has fewer than five non-zero weights. Reference values with a single capacity reduced to 0.35 and the rest typical, in task order - reduced inhibition gives 75, 88, 92, 88; reduced processing speed gives 81, 93, 86, 96; reduced updating gives 96, 91, 76, 86; reduced sustained effort gives 86, 88, 84, 91. Reduced inhibition and reduced speed both make the colour-word task the lowest; reduced updating and reduced effort both make the running-total task the lowest; the tool computes this rather than asserting it. The strategy slider splits the summary score of the two timed tasks into accuracy minus 12s and speed plus 12s, where s runs from minus one to plus one, so the summary score itself never moves. Deliberate simplifications: the weights are an argument about task demands rather than measured loadings, six capacities is fewer than the literature separates, and a weighted average has no thresholds, floor or ceiling effects or interactions. Nobody performs the tasks, no standardised test, subtest or item is reproduced, and no anatomy is mentioned anywhere.
